title: In orbit, a blob of water pulls itself into a floating ball

cover.alt: An astronaut aboard the International Space Station holds a straw with a clear, wobbling ball of water stuck to its tip.

body: Molecules inside a liquid are tugged from every side by their neighbours, but those at the surface are missing neighbours on the outside, so the surface acts like a skin that tries to shrink. The shape with the least surface for a given volume is a sphere. On Earth, gravity spreads larger amounts of water into puddles, but aboard the International Space Station almost nothing opposes this **surface tension**, so loose water gathers into wobbling balls. Water's hydrogen bonds give it a stronger surface tension than most liquids: about 72.8 millinewtons per metre at 20 °C.

slides.alt: Aboard the space station, an astronaut holds a straw with a ball of water on its end, lets the ball float free in front of him, then picks it up again on the straw tip, where it wobbles.
slides.caption: On the space station, a ball of water floats free of a straw, keeps its round shape, and wobbles back into a sphere when it is caught on the straw again.
slides.music: “Kalimba Relaxation Music” Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com) · CC BY 4.0

slides.heading: Whose surface pulls hardest? Largest first
slides.explanation: Water's web of hydrogen bonds beats most common liquids. Mercury, a liquid metal, is far stronger still: about 486.5 mN/m.

slides.heading: Why a sphere?
slides.text: A molecule at the surface has fewer neighbours than one inside, which leaves it with more energy. A liquid settles into its lowest-energy state by keeping as few molecules as possible at the surface, and for a fixed amount of liquid, no shape has less surface than a sphere.

slides.question: Water's surface tension changes with temperature. What happens between 0 °C and 100 °C?
options: It falls by about a fifth
slides.explanation: Measured values: about 75.6 mN/m at 0 °C, 72.0 at 25 °C and 58.9 at 100 °C. Hot water still pulls itself into balls, just a little less tightly.
